findings.title: minimumTokenResponseSchema uses broken computed property keys, stripping all fields except access_token
findings.body: The schema is built with `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. Calling `.toString()` on a Zod schema instance does not produce a dynamic/catch-all key based on the input data - it returns a fixed literal string (effectively the default `Object.prototype.toString()` output, the same value for both computed keys). The resulting zod object schema therefore only actually validates `access_token` plus one bogus, never-matching literal key. Because `z.object()` strips unknown keys by default (no `.passthrough()`), every other field in the token response (`expiry_date`, `refresh_token`, `expires_in`, etc.) is silently dropped from the parsed result whenever the minimum schema is used (i.e. whenever `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED && CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` are set). This corrupts the stored credential object (fields are lost) and, combined with the refresh_token fallback a few lines below, actively destroys real refresh tokens, breaking the very feature this PR implements.

findings.title: Fallback overwrites real refresh_token with the literal string "refresh_token"
findings.body: When `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token` is falsy (e.g. because the schema stripped it, or because the provider legitimately omits refresh_token on refresh responses - several providers, including Office365 whose schema marks `refresh_token` as optional, do not always return a new refresh_token), this code assigns the literal string `"refresh_token"` as the refresh token value. That bogus placeholder then gets persisted to the credential's `key` in the database, permanently destroying the real refresh token and breaking all subsequent token refreshes for that credential until the user re-authenticates. This can happen even without the new credential-sync feature enabled, as a regression for any provider whose refresh endpoint omits refresh_token.

findings.title: Sync-endpoint response shape does not match what several callers expect, causing runtime failures
findings.body: When credential sync is enabled, this function returns the raw, un-parsed `fetch` `Response` object from `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. However several callers assume a different shape depending on their normal (non-sync) refresh implementation: GoogleCalendarService reads `res?.data` (expecting an axios/googleapis-style response), HubspotCalendarService reads properties like `.expiresIn`/`.accessToken` directly off the return value (expecting an already-parsed `HubspotToken` object), and the Zoho-Bigin/ZohoCRM CalendarServices read `tokenInfo.data` (expecting an axios response). None of these properties exist on a raw fetch `Response`, so when sync mode is enabled these integrations will silently receive `undefined` values (NaN expiry dates, undefined access tokens) or throw, and then typically fail to persist anything useful, breaking token refresh for these providers under the very feature this PR adds.

findings.title: Outgoing credential-sync request has no HTTP status check and no built-in authentication
findings.body: The POST request made to `process.env.CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` carries no authentication header/secret from Cal.com's side (only `calcomUserId` and `appSlug` in the body), and the response is returned and used regardless of `response.ok`. A failing or malicious response at this endpoint (e.g. a 4xx/5xx or an endpoint that answers unauthenticated) would be treated as a successful token refresh, and the self-hosted receiving endpoint has no way to verify the request actually originated from the paired Cal.com deployment, since no shared secret is sent.

findings.title: appStoreMetadata is looked up by app.slug, but the generated metadata map is keyed by app directory name, not slug
findings.body: `appStoreMetadata` is generated by scanning app-store directories and is keyed by each app's folder/dirName (e.g. `office365video`, `googlecalendar`, `zoomvideo`, `larkcalendar`), while `app.slug` (and `reqBody.appSlug`) is the user-facing slug stored on the `App` model, which frequently differs from the directory name (e.g. slug `msteams` for dir `office365video`, slug `google-calendar` for dir `googlecalendar`, slug `zoom` for dir `zoomvideo`, slug `lark-calendar` for dir `larkcalendar`). Indexing `appStoreMetadata` with `app.slug` will return `undefined` for most of these apps, causing the handler to incorrectly respond with 404 "App not found" even though the app and slug are valid, breaking credential sync for the majority of the apps this PR claims to support.

findings.title: Webhook secret comparison is not constant-time
findings.body: The webhook secret check uses plain `!==` string comparison between the request header and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. This is vulnerable to timing attacks that could help an attacker brute-force the secret byte-by-byte. Given that a correct secret grants the ability to create/overwrite arbitrary users' third-party credentials (full account/app takeover), this comparison should use a constant-time equality check (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`).

findings.title: Unvalidated request body/decryption can throw unhandled exceptions
findings.body: `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` uses `.parse` (which throws on invalid input) instead of `.safeParse`, and there is no try/catch around it or around `JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...))` further down. A malformed request body or payload that fails decryption/JSON parsing will throw an uncaught exception inside the handler instead of returning a controlled 400 response, and the handler also never checks `req.method`, so non-POST requests are processed the same way.

findings.title: Credential lookup via findFirst can target the wrong credential when multiple exist for the same app/user
findings.body: The handler finds an existing credential with `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` and, if found, overwrites its `key`. Several apps (e.g. Google Calendar) support installing multiple credentials of the same type for one user. `findFirst` with no explicit ordering can return any one of them non-deterministically, so this sync could silently overwrite the wrong one of a user's multiple connected accounts for the same app.

findings.title: Salesforce token refresh was not wired up to the new credential-sync mechanism
findings.body: Unlike every other provider touched by this PR (Google Calendar, Office365, Hubspot, Zoom, Webex, Lark, Zoho CRM/Bigin), the newly added Salesforce refresh-token logic calls `fetch("https://login.salesforce.com/services/oauth2/token", ...)` directly instead of going through `refreshOAuthTokens`. As a result, enabling `APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED`/`CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` has no effect for Salesforce credentials; they will always be refreshed against Salesforce directly, contradicting the PR's stated goal of letting self-hosters' app store be the source of truth for all apps, and nothing in the PR description calls out this exclusion.

findings.title: Unrelated change replaces dynamic redirect URI with a hardcoded slug
findings.body: This line was changed from `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/${appConfig.slug}/callback\`` to the hardcoded `WEBAPP_URL + \`/api/integrations/zoho-bigin/callback\``. This is unrelated to the credential-sync feature described in the PR, and it introduces maintenance drift risk: if `appConfig.slug` in `config.json` is ever updated, this redirect URI will silently stop matching the app's configured slug, instead of automatically staying in sync.
